data.title: Website strategy
data.excerpt: Start with the people your website needs to help. We turn audience questions, business priorities and existing content into a clear page plan.
data.image_alt: Illustrative studio workspace with website concepts on desktop and laptop screens

children.text: Putting it into practice

The first deliverable is a practical brief: who each page serves, what it needs to explain and the action a visitor should be able to take. Reviewing this together keeps design decisions tied to a shared purpose.

data.title: Brand and interface design
data.excerpt: A recognisable website needs more than a logo. Colour, typography, photography and interaction should feel like parts of the same business.
data.image_alt: Website design palette and visual system demonstration

children.text: Putting it into practice
We explore the key pages before extending the visual language across the site. This gives your team something concrete to review and leaves a small, useful set of design rules for future content.

data.title: Website development
data.excerpt: A good design should remain useful after launch. We build pages around editable sections so your team can keep services, people and news up to date.
data.image_alt: Website design palette and visual system demonstration

children.text: Putting it into practice
We review navigation, forms and layouts with realistic content on small and large screens. Handover includes a walk-through of the pages your team will change most often.

data.title: Content and photography
data.excerpt: Specific words and relevant images help people understand what you do. We plan content around customer questions and choose visuals that explain the work.
data.image_alt: Website design palette and visual system demonstration

children.text: Putting it into practice

The content plan identifies the message, image and next step for each section. Photographs should show the product, process or people behind the service; captions provide context rather than repeat the headline.

data.title: Website care
data.excerpt: Websites need attention as a business changes. A regular review helps keep contact information, services, software and the visitor journey current.
data.image_alt: Illustrative studio workspace with website concepts on desktop and laptop screens

children.text: Putting it into practice
Begin with a list of important pages and forms. Record what changed, check the result on a phone and keep a recovery point before technical updates. Agree who receives and follows up on enquiries.

data.title: Planning a focused campaign page
data.excerpt: A campaign page works best when its offer and audience are specific. The headline, supporting detail and action should all serve that one purpose.
data.image_alt: Sample image

children.text: Putting it into practice
Match the promise in the campaign message to the landing page. Remove distracting detours, explain the next step and confirm that enquiries reach the right person.

data.title: Website design and build
data.excerpt: A connected service for planning your website, shaping its visual identity and building pages your team can maintain.

children.text: From the brief to a working website
Start with the audience and the questions your site needs to answer. Review the key pages, agree the content and test the customer journey before launch.
What we work through together
A focused brief and page plan
Visual direction and page concepts
Editable content, images and section layouts
Desktop and mobile review
An editing walk-through and handover checklist

faq_items.question: What is included in the service?
faq_items.answer: Scope is agreed around your audience, content and the pages you need. A written brief records the deliverables.

faq_items.question: How do reviews work?
faq_items.answer: Review the work at agreed checkpoints and collect feedback in one place. Decisions stay connected to the purpose of each page.

faq_items.question: What happens after handover?
faq_items.answer: Your team receives an editing walk-through and a clear list of next steps. Ongoing support can be scoped separately.

data.cta_statement: Tell us what your next website needs to do.
data.cta_support: Bring the idea, the existing site or the question you have not answered yet. Start with a conversation.

data.title: Adam Hale — Design Director
data.name: Adam Hale
data.excerpt: Adam Hale is the demo studio’s design director. This profile illustrates how a team page can connect a person’s role with the work customers care about.
data.image_alt: Illustrative portrait for the fictional studio team

children.text: Putting it into practice

In this sample team, Adam Hale leads visual direction and reviews page concepts with clients. Replace this fictional biography and its illustrative portrait with your own team’s experience before publishing.

data.title: Peter Lang — Development Lead
data.name: Peter Lang
data.excerpt: Peter Lang is the demo studio’s development lead, responsible for turning agreed designs into editable, maintainable pages.
data.image_alt: Illustrative portrait for the fictional studio team

children.text: Putting it into practice
This fictional profile shows a concise way to describe a technical role without listing every tool. For your own team, add the responsibilities and experience that are relevant to customers.

data.title: Sofia Lindqvist — Brand Designer
data.name: Sofia Lindqvist
data.excerpt: Sofia Lindqvist is the demo studio’s brand designer, connecting visual identity, photography and written content across the customer journey.
data.image_alt: Illustrative portrait for the fictional studio team

children.text: Putting it into practice
This is an illustrative biography. Replace the name, role and portrait together, then add one specific example of the work your colleague contributes to a project.

data.title: Lucas Meyer — Research Lead
data.name: Lucas Meyer
data.excerpt: Lucas Meyer is the demo studio’s research lead, bringing customer questions into the project before the page designs are final.
data.image_alt: Illustrative portrait for the fictional studio team

children.text: Putting it into practice

This fictional profile illustrates a research role through its purpose: helping a team make informed decisions. A real biography can include relevant experience and the ways clients work with that person.

data.title: Writing a useful website brief
data.excerpt: A useful brief explains the business problem before listing page features. Describe your audience, the questions they ask and what a successful visit looks like.
data.image_alt: Planning ideas on a wall of project notes
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Include existing pages, content owners and examples with a sentence explaining what you like about each. Separate essentials from ideas that can wait so the project has a clear first release.

data.title: Designing a contact page people can use
data.excerpt: Someone arriving at a contact page is ready for a next step. Make the available channels and the information you need easy to understand.
data.image_alt: Website design workspace with sketches and screens
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Keep required fields to a minimum. Explain what happens after submission and test where the message is delivered. An attractive form is only useful when a person can receive and respond to it.

data.title: Editing website copy for clarity
data.excerpt: Clear copy helps people decide whether a service fits their needs. Start with the answer a visitor came for, then add enough detail to support it.
data.image_alt: A reader reviewing content on a laptop
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Replace broad promises with specific descriptions of the work. Read headings on their own: they should still explain the page’s structure and lead towards a useful next step.

data.title: Choosing what belongs on the homepage
data.excerpt: A homepage introduces the business and helps visitors choose where to go. It does not need to contain every detail from every service.
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Prioritise the audience, offer, proof and next step. Link to deeper pages for process and scope, and remove sections that repeat the same message without adding evidence.

data.title: Building an editorial calendar
data.excerpt: A small, sustainable editorial plan is more useful than an ambitious calendar nobody owns. Begin with questions customers already ask.
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Assign a purpose, owner and review date to each article. Balance practical guidance with business updates, and revisit older posts when services or processes change.

data.title: Making service pages more specific
data.excerpt: A service name alone rarely tells a customer what they are buying. Explain the problem, the work involved and the outcome they can review.
data.image_alt: Website wireframes and layout sketches on a design desk
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Include scope, typical inputs and the next conversation. Be clear about what varies by project instead of promising one timeline or price for every situation.

data.title: Writing headings that guide a reader
data.excerpt: Headings are a navigation system inside a page. They should tell a reader what the next section will help them understand.
data.image_alt: A woman reading on a laptop in a cafe
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Use a clear hierarchy and descriptive language. Check how longer headings wrap on a phone and avoid relying on visual size alone to communicate their level.

data.title: Using customer stories responsibly
data.excerpt: A useful customer story explains the starting point, the work and what changed. Specific evidence is more convincing than a collection of superlatives.
data.image_alt: A thank-you card resting on a gift box
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Ask permission before publishing names, logos or quotes. Keep results in context and label illustrative examples so readers can distinguish them from verified customer work.

data.title: A simple content review workflow
data.excerpt: A review workflow should make it clear who checks accuracy, who approves wording and who publishes. Too many parallel copies make that harder.
data.image_alt: A planning board with notes grouped for review
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Work from a single draft, collect comments in one place and record the approval. After publishing, check the live page and set a date to review time-sensitive details.

data.title: Choosing a CMS your team can use
data.excerpt: A CMS decision should include the people who will maintain the website. The best fit depends on their everyday tasks as much as the feature list.
data.image_alt: Illustrative studio workspace with website concepts on desktop and laptop screens
data.author: Demo User

children.text: Putting it into practice
Try representative edits before committing: change a service, replace an image and publish a post. Review permissions, support and the effort required to keep the platform current.

data.title: Asking better questions about hosting
data.excerpt: Hosting supports the website’s availability, updates and recovery. Compare responsibilities and support arrangements alongside capacity and price.
data.image_alt: Illustrative studio workspace with website concepts on desktop and laptop screens
data.author: Demo User

children.text: Putting it into practice
Ask how backups are restored, who handles incidents and what access the owner receives. Keep a written record of the arrangement so responsibilities remain clear after launch.

data.title: Preparing an asset inventory
data.excerpt: An asset inventory connects every photograph, document and logo to its purpose. It helps a team spot missing materials before pages are built.
data.image_alt: Website design workspace with sketches and screens
data.author: Demo User

children.text: Putting it into practice
Record the owner, usage permission and intended page for each asset. Keep originals separate from web exports and use descriptive filenames that the next editor can recognise.

data.title: Reviewing third-party integrations
data.excerpt: Each integration adds a dependency to the website. Map the data it receives and the task it serves before deciding whether to include it.
data.image_alt: Working at a desktop and laptop workstation
data.author: Demo User

children.text: Putting it into practice
Test failure states as well as successful requests. Identify who owns the external account, how access is managed and what the visitor sees when the service is unavailable.

data.title: Comparing proposals on the same basis
data.excerpt: Website proposals become easier to compare when they describe the same scope. A headline price can hide different assumptions about content and support.
data.author: Demo User

children.text: Putting it into practice
Ask for deliverables, review rounds, responsibilities and handover details. Separate recurring costs from project work and clarify how changes to the brief will be handled.

data.title: Making recovery part of launch planning
data.excerpt: A recovery plan describes how a site gets back to a known working state. Keeping a backup is one step; testing its restoration is another.
data.image_alt: Hard drive used to illustrate website backup storage
data.author: Lawrence

children.text: Putting it into practice
Record where copies are stored and who can restore them. Practise on an isolated environment and confirm that content, media and forms work after the restoration.

data.title: A routine for website updates
data.excerpt: Updates are easier to manage when they follow a repeatable routine. A small checklist helps prevent the same important checks being forgotten.
data.image_alt: Working at a desktop and laptop workstation
data.author: Lawrence

children.text: Putting it into practice
Take a recovery point, review changes on a preview and test key journeys. Record the version and result, then monitor the live site after the update.

data.title: Keeping forms connected to your team
data.excerpt: Forms are part of an operational process, not just page decoration. A message needs a destination and someone responsible for answering it.
data.image_alt: Reviewing website content on a laptop
data.author: Lawrence

children.text: Putting it into practice
Send a test enquiry through each important form and confirm receipt. Check spam handling and response ownership, and repeat the test after changes to email services.

data.title: Reading website analytics with a purpose
data.excerpt: Analytics are useful when they answer a business question. A large report is less helpful than a small set of measures the team understands.
data.image_alt: Data charts on a computer display
data.author: Lawrence

children.text: Putting it into practice
Choose the journeys you want to improve and look for points where people stop. Combine the numbers with customer feedback before deciding what to change.

data.title: Reducing unnecessary page weight
data.excerpt: Page weight often grows one small addition at a time. Images, fonts and optional widgets should each earn their place in the visitor experience.
data.image_alt: Website design workspace with sketches and screens
data.author: Lawrence

children.text: Putting it into practice
Review the largest assets first and remove features that no longer serve a purpose. Check the result on a typical phone connection instead of relying only on a fast office network.

data.title: Studio notes: starting with the customer
data.excerpt: This sample studio update introduces a customer-centred way of planning a website. It shows how a short company post can share a useful lesson.
data.image_alt: A business owner working on a laptop
data.author: Damon Zemlak

children.text: Putting it into practice
For your own business, describe a recent observation, what your team changed and why. Add a relevant photograph and keep client details private unless you have permission to share them.

data.title: Studio notes: a better project kickoff
data.excerpt: A project kickoff is a chance to align people before work starts. This illustrative update focuses on making responsibilities and decisions visible.
data.image_alt: Planning ideas on a wall of project notes
data.author: Damon Zemlak

children.text: Putting it into practice
An effective recap can record the purpose, participants and next actions without publishing confidential details. Replace this demo story with an update from your own team.

data.title: Studio notes: reviewing work together
data.excerpt: This demo article presents a collaborative review session. The emphasis is on the question the team is trying to answer, not the number of screens produced.
data.image_alt: Working at a desktop and laptop workstation
data.author: Damon Zemlak

children.text: Putting it into practice
Use your own update to explain one decision and how feedback informed it. A short account with a relevant image often tells readers more than a broad claim about creativity.

data.title: Studio notes: welcoming a new perspective
data.excerpt: A team update can introduce the contribution a person brings to the business. This is an example story, not a real hiring announcement.
data.image_alt: Reviewing website content on a laptop
data.author: Damon Zemlak

children.text: Putting it into practice
When publishing your own version, include the person’s role, a short biography and an approved portrait. Confirm names and links with the person before the page goes live.

data.title: Studio notes: making time for improvements
data.excerpt: Not every business update needs to announce a new product. Small improvements to how a team works can be useful stories in their own right.
data.image_alt: Website design workspace with sketches and screens
data.author: Damon Zemlak

children.text: Putting it into practice
Choose one change, describe the reason for it and explain who it helps. Replace this illustrative post with a specific example from your organisation.

data.title: Testing a website before launch
data.excerpt: A launch check should follow the journeys that matter: learning about a service, reading details, finding contact information and making an enquiry.
data.image_alt: Sample image
data.author: Jesus Hessel

children.text: Putting it into practice
Check links and forms with realistic text, including long names and messages. Review both appearance and delivery, and record who signs off each journey.

data.title: Planning a website migration
data.excerpt: Moving a website changes more than its files. Existing URLs, media, search traffic and editorial habits all need a place in the plan.
data.image_alt: Sample image
data.author: Jesus Hessel

children.text: Putting it into practice
Inventory the current pages and map each important URL to its destination. Test redirects and forms on a preview, keep a recovery copy and schedule a review after the move.

data.title: Keeping images sharp on smaller screens
data.excerpt: An image that works across a desktop banner may lose its subject in a phone crop. Choose the focal point before exporting the final sizes.
data.image_alt: A desk arranged for digital design work
data.author: Jesus Hessel

children.text: Putting it into practice
Keep essential details away from the edges. Supply dimensions with the image, use an appropriate file size and check the actual crop beside its heading on a narrow screen.

data.title: Making a website easy to maintain
data.excerpt: Maintenance becomes easier when each piece of content has a clear home. Repeated copy and unclear section names make routine edits harder than they need to be.
data.image_alt: A laptop on a desk beside a window
data.author: Jesus Hessel

children.text: Putting it into practice
Name sections by page and purpose, keep shared content in one place and write a short editing guide. Test the guide with someone who did not build the site.

data.title: A practical handover checklist
data.excerpt: A website handover should give the owner confidence to make everyday changes. Access credentials alone do not explain how the site is organised.
data.image_alt: A planning board with grouped handover notes
data.author: Jesus Hessel

children.text: Putting it into practice
Walk through changing a service, replacing a photograph and publishing a post. Record the support contact and recovery process, and confirm that the owner can complete those tasks.

data.title: Testing keyboard navigation
data.excerpt: A visitor should be able to follow the main journey with a keyboard. Menus, links and forms need a clear focus indicator and a sensible order.
data.image_alt: Sample image
data.author: Jesus Hessel

children.text: Putting it into practice
Move through the page without a mouse. Check that overlays can be closed and focused controls remain visible, then record problems against the exact page and control.

data.title: Inside a collaborative design review
data.excerpt: A design review works best when everyone is responding to the same question. A focused session is more useful than a long list of unrelated preferences.
data.image_alt: Sample demo image
data.author: Frederik Herzog

children.text: Putting it into practice
Share the goal and pages in advance. Discuss clarity, hierarchy and the next action, then record decisions in one place with a named owner for each follow-up.

data.title: Preparing for a team photo session
data.excerpt: Team photographs feel more natural when people know how the images will be used. Plan portraits, group scenes and working details as separate needs.
data.image_alt: Colleagues working together in a studio
data.author: Frederik Herzog

children.text: Putting it into practice
Choose a consistent light and background for portraits. Leave room for different crops and ask for permission to use each image on the website and related materials.

data.title: A workspace that supports creative work
data.excerpt: A workspace tells part of a studio’s story. Useful photographs show how people collaborate and what they make, rather than only furniture and decoration.
data.image_alt: Demo image
data.author: Frederik Herzog

children.text: Putting it into practice
Capture a mix of wide scenes and close details. Avoid displaying private client material on screens or printouts, and give each image a caption that explains its context.

data.title: From workshop notes to a page plan
data.excerpt: A workshop often produces more ideas than a first website release can contain. The next step is to turn those notes into a useful order.
data.image_alt: Demo image
data.author: Frederik Herzog

children.text: Putting it into practice
Group questions by audience need. Give each proposed page one main purpose, mark the content owner and identify what must be ready before design starts.

data.title: Organising a useful inspiration library
data.excerpt: An inspiration library helps when its examples have context. A folder of unexplained screenshots is difficult for another person to use.
data.image_alt: Design materials arranged on a workspace
data.author: Frederik Herzog

children.text: Putting it into practice
Group examples by the problem they address and add a short note about what is useful. Keep references separate from finished brand assets so they are not mistaken for approved work.

data.title: Keeping project decisions findable
data.excerpt: A decision is easier to follow when its reason is recorded with it. Clear notes prevent a team from repeating the same discussion later.
data.image_alt: Sample demo image
data.author: Frederik Herzog

children.text: Putting it into practice
Write down the question, the choice and its practical consequence. Link to the relevant page or design and update the note when the decision changes.

data.title: Making room for informal conversations
data.excerpt: Informal conversations can reveal questions that never appear in a project document. This demo article shows a lighter side of studio life.
data.image_alt: Demo image
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
For a real company update, use a photograph from your own gathering and explain its context. Avoid turning a casual moment into an unsupported claim about workplace culture.

data.title: A team lunch with a purpose
data.excerpt: Shared meals can be a simple opportunity for a team to reconnect. This illustrative article provides a layout for a short people-focused update.
data.image_alt: Demo image
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Tell readers what happened and why it mattered to the people involved. Use approved photographs, name participants accurately and keep the story proportionate to the occasion.

data.title: Collecting inspiration outside the studio
data.excerpt: Observation away from a screen can offer a fresh perspective on a design problem. This sample post introduces an inspiration journal format.
data.image_alt: Sample image
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
Show a few details, describe what caught your attention and connect the observation to your work. Credit the place or creator where appropriate.

data.title: Sharing knowledge in small sessions
data.excerpt: A short internal session can make one useful skill easier for everyone to practise. This fictional update illustrates a learning activity.
data.image_alt: Sample demo image
data.author: Tracy Agent

children.text: Putting it into practice
In a real post, explain the topic and share one takeaway readers can use. Include a resource only when it is relevant and available to the audience.

data.title: How the demo team works together
data.excerpt: The four fictional team members represent design, development, brand and research. Their roles show how a business can explain its working relationships.
data.image_alt: Sample image
data.author: Gerson Jacobson

children.text: Putting it into practice
Use this page to describe your own team’s responsibilities and how customers interact with them. Replace demo identities and portraits before presenting the site as your business.

data.title: Meet the people behind a project
data.excerpt: A team page can do more than list job titles. It can help visitors understand who they will work with and what each person contributes.
data.author: Gerson Jacobson

children.text: Putting it into practice
Start with a consistent profile format: name, role, relevant experience and a short personal detail if the person is comfortable sharing it.

faq_items.question: Where does a website project start?
faq_items.answer: Start with the audience, the main offer and the questions customers ask. These shape the brief and page plan.

faq_items.question: Can our team update the content?
faq_items.answer: The demo uses editable content and page sections in the admin. Your team can replace words, images, links and section content through the admin.

faq_items.question: What do we need to prepare?
faq_items.answer: Bring your service information, brand assets and photographs you have permission to use. Agree who will review and approve the content.

faq_items.question: How are scope and pricing agreed?
faq_items.answer: Confirm the deliverables, responsibilities and support needed for your project. The plans on this demo are illustrative examples.

faq_items.question: Can you work with an existing website?
faq_items.answer: An existing site can provide useful content and evidence about the customer journey. Review what to keep before deciding what to change.

data.services_title: One connected service. From idea to everyday use.
data.services_lead: Bring us a new idea, an existing website or a question about what comes next.

services_items.title: Website strategy
services_items.text: Start with the people your website needs to help. We turn audience questions, business priorities and existing content into a clear page plan.

services_items.title: Brand and interface design
services_items.text: A recognisable website needs more than a logo. Colour, typography, photography and interaction should feel like parts of the same business.

services_items.title: Website development
services_items.text: A good design should remain useful after launch. We build pages around editable sections so your team can keep services, people and news up to date.

services_items.title: Content and photography
services_items.text: Specific words and relevant images help people understand what you do. We plan content around customer questions and choose visuals that explain the work.

services_items.title: Website care
services_items.text: Websites need attention as a business changes. A regular review helps keep contact information, services, software and the visitor journey current.

services_items.title: Planning a focused campaign page
services_items.text: A campaign page works best when its offer and audience are specific. The headline, supporting detail and action should all serve that one purpose.

data.product_title: A website your team can keep moving.
data.product_lead: The result is more than a launch-day design: a shared foundation for the work that comes after it.

product_parts.title: A consistent design system
product_parts.text: Shared colour, type and layout rules help every service page, article and campaign feel like part of the same business.

product_parts.title: Content that stays editable
product_parts.text: Reusable page sections give the team a clear place to update a service, introduce a colleague or publish the next story.

product_parts.title: A clear way to keep improving
product_parts.text: Use the handover, review checklist and content plan to decide what to change next, without starting the whole site again.

data.process_lead: A clear brief, visible decisions and a handover that leaves the team ready to work.

process_steps.title: Discover the business
process_steps.text: Map the audience, offer and customer questions before deciding what each page needs.

process_steps.title: Shape the experience
process_steps.text: Bring the message, visual identity and page structure together in concrete page concepts.

process_steps.title: Build and review
process_steps.text: Turn the agreed direction into editable pages and review the important visitor journeys.

process_steps.title: Launch and learn
process_steps.text: Hand over the content workflow and use regular reviews to keep the website useful.

faq_items.question: What can a project include?
faq_items.answer: A project can connect website strategy, content planning, identity, interface design and development. The brief defines which parts the business needs.

faq_items.question: Can we start with an existing website?
faq_items.answer: Yes. Start by reviewing the content, page structure and customer journeys. That review helps separate what is useful from what needs to change.

faq_items.question: Will our team be able to edit the content?
faq_items.answer: The demo uses editable content and page sections in the admin. A handover can explain where the different sections live and how to keep them current.

faq_items.question: How do we decide the scope?
faq_items.answer: Bring the existing site, the goals and the questions you have. The first step is to agree priorities, deliverables and responsibilities.

faq_items.question: What happens after launch?
faq_items.answer: Keep a list of customer questions and content changes. Regular reviews help the website follow the business as it grows and changes.
